'Abstract' section.text:
A production agent loop that does not name its stop conditions spends until a person notices. [3]

This paper separates one reference implementation's three exits from the turn and recursion limits documented by two agent runtimes. [1][2][3]

The reference loop checks done, then cost, then max turns. That order is a local policy on a single source, not a vendor standard. [1]

Claude Agent SDK documents a turn cap as max_turns. Deep Agents documents a recursion limit as the graph boundary. Each of those statements rests on a single source. [2][3]

The paper then asks what changes when verification is a different role with a different tool scope, rather than another self-reflection turn by the same actor. [4][5]

The finding is narrow. A host that wants a bounded loop has to put the bound in the program. A host that wants independent verification has to split the tools. Neither property appears because a model was told to be careful. [1][4]

'Introduction' section.text:
An agent loop is a program that calls a model, acts on the reply, and repeats. The repetition is useful only when its stopping boundary is explicit. [3]

A graph without that boundary can continue indefinitely. The Deep Agents overview states the graph stops when it reaches its recursion limit. That is a runtime detail on a single source, not a general result about agent systems. [3]

The alternative is to leave stopping to the model's own judgment. A model that is asked whether it is done can talk itself past the stop. A documented recursion limit is a program bound. It is also only one bound, and it is not a cost bound. [3]

A host that copies only a recursion limit gets a stack bound. Recursion is not a cost bound, and it is not a success bound. A run that is not done, is not out of money, and is not out of turns should take the next turn. Anything else is a fourth exit invented in prose. [3]

The rest of this paper stays inside that claim. It names the vendor limit as documented behavior for that runtime. It does not measure production loops, and it does not claim a standard. [3]

A brief can stop after naming a recursion limit. A paper has to say what that limit is for, what it is not, and what a host gives up by copying only a vendor page. That is the difference this pipeline is supposed to produce. [3]

The reader this paper assumes is an engineer who already runs an agent loop against a real bill. The paper does not teach how to call a model. It teaches where the stop lives, and why putting that stop in a prompt is not the same as putting it in the program. [3]

The Saturday lab already produces a cited brief. That brief is the right size for a workshop afternoon. This take-home is supposed to produce a document a colleague can use without sitting next to the author. The extra length is mechanism, tradeoff, and limit, not a longer restatement of the same vendor sentence. [3]

A graph that hits recursion while the work is half written has stopped for a reason a cost cap would not have used first. The host that wants cost and done as well still has to add those checks. The vendor page does not add them. [3]

If the recursion component is missing, the bound disappears with it. The rest of the system can still call a model and act on the reply. The loop continues until an operator notices. That is the failure the explicit boundary exists to prevent. [3]

'Exit conditions' section.text:
The Sol3 reference implementation checks three exits in order: done, then cost, then max turns. [1]

Done is first because a finished run is a finished run. A paper that already passed its gates is not discarded because a later accounting pass noticed the budget. Cost is second because another model call after the money is gone is how a cap turns into a multiplier. Max turns is last because a loop that is not converging should hit money before it hits a turn counter, and the turn counter is the backstop when money is still left. [1]

That order is a design policy in the reference implementation. It is not a claim that vendors standardize the same three conditions. The implementation records the reason it stopped, and a later resume reads that reason instead of guessing. [1]

The Claude Agent SDK exposes a turn cap as max_turns. On a single source, that is documented behavior for that runtime, not a portable exit doctrine. A host that sets max_turns and nothing else has a turn bound. It does not have a cost bound, and it does not have a success bound named done. [2]

Deep Agents documents a recursion limit as the graph boundary. On a single source, that is a stack bound for that graph. Recursion depth is not cost, and it is not done. A graph that hits recursion while the paper is half written has stopped for a reason the reference loop would not have used first. [3]

The alternative to these three is a single vendor limit, or a model-owned stop. A single vendor limit is cheaper to configure. Its cost is that the reason the run stopped is whatever that runtime happened to check, which may not be the reason a person would have chosen. A model-owned stop is cheaper still. Its cost is that the model can talk past it. [1][2][3]

The mechanism in the reference loop is a function that takes done, spent money, the cap, and whether turns are exhausted. It returns stop and a reason. Callers check that return before the next stage, not after. Checking after is how a stage that loops over six sections makes six calls with nothing between them. [1]

A stage that is expensive should checkpoint after each unit, not after the stage. A write stage that persists only on success makes a mid-stage stop cost the whole stage again. That is the opposite of what a cost cap is for. The three exits only work if the loop consults them at the unit boundary. [1]

Resume is part of the same mechanism. A failed stage is not a finished stage. A second run that skips a failed stage hides the failure. A second run that reruns a finished stage spends money to risk breaking it. The state file is what makes those two cases distinguishable without asking a model. [1]

Stable failure is the one extra case the loop catches on purpose. Two rounds with the same missing-field signature are not converging. Retrying them spends the last attempt to watch the same failure again. The loop escalates instead. That is still not a fourth exit. It is the turn cap firing early because the signature did not move. [1]

The limit of this evidence is the implementation itself plus two vendor pages. No production loop was measured. No cost figures in this paper come from a live bill. Treat the three exits as the local doctrine, and treat the vendor limits as documented behavior for those runtimes. [1][2][3]

'Independent verification' section.text:
The agent-loop guidance says verification works best when the verifier does not share the actor's context. [4]

That is a structural claim, not a prompt. A checker that can see the maker's scratch work will agree with the maker by construction. Two models reading one page agree. Two models holding the same tools will reach for the same repair. Independence is a tool-scope property before it is a personality property. [4]

CRITIC reports that intrinsic self-correction without external feedback rarely improves correctness. A second pass by the same actor, with the same tools, is another self-reflection turn. It is not independent validation. The paper uses that result as a motive for a maker and checker split, not as a measured result about this repository. [5]

The mechanism is therefore a role table. The writer holds a folder-limited write. The verifier holds an evidence write and is denied the paper. The reviewer holds no write at all. A role that can fix its own complaint stops reporting the complaints that are hard to fix. [4][5]

The alternative is one agent with a long prompt that says now verify your work. That alternative is cheaper. It needs no second role, no second tool list, and no path check. Its cost is that the verification is whatever the same context can see, which is the failure the split exists to prevent. [4][5]

A path check inside the write tool is what makes the table real. An instruction that says do not edit the paper is an instruction a model can reinterpret. A tool that returns a refusal sentence names the scope and changes the next action. A raw traceback in the same context starts a retry loop instead. [4]

The reviewer is the test of this design. It grades a draft against a rubric and returns failing rows. It cannot rewrite the draft. If it could, the next pass would be the reviewer agreeing with its own repair, which is the same self-correction CRITIC reports does not help. [5]

Handing the verifier the researcher's source turns an independent check into a reading-comprehension exercise. The verifier in this pipeline is given the claim text and nothing else. Agreement then has to come from a second retrieval, not from rereading the first page. [4]

The limit of this evidence is one vendor page on agent loops and one result on self-correction. Neither source measures this repository's role table. The conclusion about any specific tool scope is an engineering inference from those two claims, not a production measurement. [4][5]

'Limitations' section.text:
This paper combines one reference implementation, two runtime documents, and one paper on self-correction. [1][2][3][5]

It measures no production loops and reports no cost figures of its own. The three-exit order is the local doctrine. It is not a standard, and it is not a claim that other runtimes should copy it. [1]

The runtime limits are each single source observations. Treat them as documented behavior for those runtimes, not as a universal property of agent systems. [2][3]

The maker and checker split is motivated by CRITIC. It is not proven here. A host that wants the split still has to put it in the role table, not in the prompt. [5]

A live run against a different topic will retrieve different pages. The gates in this paper check citations, section shape, figure assets, and length. They do not check whether the argument is the one a specialist would have written. That judgment stays with the reviewer, and the reviewer can be wrong without corrupting the evidence bundle. [1][5]
